sm: The episode opens with the news. President Trump is heading to the Philippines to start an Asia trip, with talks expected on trade, nuclear weapons, Iran and Ukraine, followed by meetings in Beijing with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. The administration is also tightening Chinese access to American AI computing power. Trump and Vice President J.D. Vance spoke about Friday's nationwide ground stop, which the FAA blamed on aging equipment overwhelmed with data during a contractor's fiber optic upgrade. Vance said some equipment is as much as fifty years old, and the administration is seeking fifty billion dollars from Congress. Other stories covered a JP Morgan Chase software glitch, a third American aircraft carrier arriving near Iran, and a second trial for Lindsay Clancy set for March. The hosts then introduced Mark Scribner of the Reason Foundation to discuss the ground stop.

Mark Scribner described being in the air when the ground stop began and said the FAA offered little information at first. He said the failure affected high altitude centers and terminal control centers, though safety was not threatened because emergency procedures kicked in. He said a contractor replacing old routers overwhelmed the legacy telecommunications system, which calls into question both the contractor and FAA oversight, and he noted the agency had received about twelve billion dollars last year. He argued the current plan simply throws money at the legacy system, when air traffic control should instead be in a state of constant modernization. The show then turned to Samuel Sey, a conservative Christian commentator deported to Canada, and his friend Aaron Baer said Sey believed his paperwork was in order because he had presented it at airport security.

Aaron Baer said Samuel Sey believed he was legally in the country, and that something went wrong with his paperwork, whether through his own inaction or his attorneys. He said Sey still supports immigration enforcement and told him he sided with those who value law and order, not the protesters outside the detention facility. Baer said Sey's wife, Annie, and their three children have been supported by their church community. He said he sees no tension between enforcing the law and treating people justly, and that Sey is safe with his family in Canada while they work on bringing him back. The program then began a report on Anthropic's coming public stock offering, expected to raise up to sixty-five billion dollars, and on workers like marketing writer Ailsa Woods, who lost a job to ChatGPT.

The report said Anthropic offered three scenarios for AI's economic effect, modest, substantial and extreme, all showing net gains in productivity. In the extreme case, nearly a sixth of knowledge workers, about fourteen million people, could lose their jobs, while the economy could grow up to fifteen percent a year. Economists noted that adoption is costly, and that wages could rise even as entry level jobs become harder to find. Woods predicts people will prefer companies that do not use AI, and the report cited polls showing more than half of Americans think AI's risks outweigh its benefits. A lighter story described a gas price war in Powder Springs, Georgia, that dropped prices below one ninety-seven a gallon and caused a traffic jam. A new story then began on Jane Schlanker, who set out in the Vietnam era to join the Air Force.

Schlanker's story continued with the all-volunteer force, basic training and housing in the 1970s, and an early culture she called an old boys club where women had to do their jobs a little better than everyone else. She became the first woman to reach Chief Master Sergeant of the 442nd Fighter Wing, retired in 2002 after twenty-five years, and said she has no regrets. Commentator Janie B. Cheney then discussed Republicans looking for silver linings after their midterm losses, including remarks from Michael Knowles and Brandy Cruz. She warned that hoping Democrats will stumble is a rickety foundation for hope, comparing it to disappointments in life and to the disciples' hopes before Good Friday. She said she cannot predict politics, but joy remains the ultimate goal. The hosts closed by previewing tomorrow's Washington Wednesday segment with Hunter Baker.
